questions.stem: A patient with chronic alcohol use has a wide-based, unsteady gait but no limb dysmetria or intention tremor on finger-to-nose testing. Which cerebellar structure is most likely affected?
explanations: Lateral cerebellar hemisphere lesions affect the ipsilateral extremities, causing dysmetria and intention tremor on finger-to-nose testing, which this patient does not have.
The dentate nucleus is a deep nucleus associated with lateral hemisphere output to the limbs, not the trunk/gait pattern described.
Flocculonodular lobe lesions cause nystagmus, vertigo, and nausea/vomiting rather than an isolated gait disturbance.

Correct — the vermis (midline cerebellar structure) controls trunk and gait; its degeneration, classically from chronic alcohol use, produces truncal/gait ataxia (a wide-based, unsteady gait) without limb dysmetria, since the lateral hemispheres controlling the limbs are relatively spared.
questions.overview: The cerebellum is functionally divided into midline structures (vermis and flocculonodular lobe), which control trunk/gait/eye movements, and lateral hemispheres, which control ipsilateral limb coordination. Vermis degeneration (classically from chronic alcohol use) causes truncal/gait ataxia without limb findings, while lateral lesions cause ipsilateral dysmetria, intention tremor, and dysdiadochokinesia.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman has a two-year history of gradually worsening memory, difficulty managing her finances, and repeatedly asking the same questions. Her level of consciousness is normal, her EEG is normal, and MRI shows hippocampal atrophy. Which of the following underlying mechanisms is most likely responsible for her symptoms?
options: Extracellular amyloid-beta plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau
Cortical accumulation of alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies
explanations: Prion-mediated spongiform change describes Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, which causes rapidly progressive dementia over weeks to months with myoclonus, not a gradual 2-year course.

Correct — Alzheimer's disease, the most common cause of dementia, is pathologically defined by extracellular amyloid (senile) plaques from abnormal APP cleavage and intraneuronal neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau, with cholinergic neuron loss (basal nucleus of Meynert) and hippocampal atrophy causing gradual memory and executive decline.
TDP-43 inclusions characterize frontotemporal dementia, which usually presents earlier (before age 65) with personality change or language impairment rather than isolated memory loss.
Stepwise vascular infarcts describe vascular dementia, which has an abrupt, stepwise decline rather than the gradual progressive course described here.

Alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies in the cortex characterize dementia with Lewy bodies, which typically features fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism, not this isolated gradual memory-predominant pattern.
questions.overview: Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia and is pathologically defined by extracellular beta-amyloid plaques (from abnormal APP cleavage, worsened by ApoE4 and protected by ApoE2) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau, with degeneration of cholinergic neurons in the basal nucleus of Meynert and hippocampal atrophy. Clinically it causes gradual, irreversible decline in short-term memory and executive function with a normal EEG, distinguishing it from delirium.

questions.stem: A farmer presents with wheezing, diarrhea, urinary incontinence, pinpoint pupils, and profuse sweating and salivation after pesticide exposure. Which drug should be given first?
explanations: Pralidoxime regenerates acetylcholinesterase but should be given after atropine, since giving it first can transiently worsen cholinergic symptoms.
Neostigmine is also an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (used for ileus/myasthenia), which would exacerbate cholinergic excess in this patient rather than treat it.
Physostigmine is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used to treat anticholinergic toxicity, not organophosphate (cholinergic) poisoning — it would worsen this patient's symptoms.

Correct — atropine is a muscarinic antagonist and first-line therapy for organophosphate (cholinergic) toxicity, rapidly reversing bradycardia, bronchorrhea, and hypotension; it has no effect at nicotinic receptors.
questions.overview: Organophosphate poisoning inhibits acetylcholinesterase, causing accumulation of acetylcholine and a cholinergic toxidrome remembered as DUMBELS (Defecation, Urination, Miosis, Bronchospasm/Bradycardia, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation). First-line treatment is atropine (a muscarinic antagonist), followed by pralidoxime, which reactivates acetylcholinesterase.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man presents with progressive chorea, irritability, and early psychiatric symptoms. Genetic testing reveals an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat. What is the primary pathophysiologic mechanism of his movement symptoms?
options: Copper accumulation in the basal ganglia
Autoimmune destruction of the subthalamic nucleus
Loss of GABAergic and cholinergic neurons in the striatum, causing indirect pathway underactivity
Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra
explanations: Copper accumulation in the basal ganglia describes Wilson disease, which causes a wing-beating tremor and dysarthria, not CAG-repeat-driven chorea.

Huntington disease is a genetic trinucleotide repeat disorder, not an autoimmune process, and it primarily affects the striatum rather than the subthalamic nucleus (whose damage causes hemiballismus).

Correct — Huntington disease is caused by CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion, leading to degeneration of striatal GABAergic and cholinergic neurons; loss of the indirect pathway's inhibitory tone disinhibits the thalamus, producing hyperkinetic chorea.
Loss of dopaminergic substantia nigra neurons describes Parkinson disease, which causes hypokinesia (bradykinesia, rigidity) — the opposite pattern of chorea.
questions.overview: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene, leading to degeneration of striatal (caudate/putamen) GABAergic and cholinergic neurons. Loss of the indirect pathway's inhibitory tone disinhibits the thalamus, producing chorea, along with progressive psychiatric symptoms and dementia; genetic anticipation causes earlier and worse onset in successive generations.

questions.stem: Which thalamic nucleus relays pain, temperature, touch, proprioception, and vibration information from the body to the somatosensory cortex?
explanations: Correct — the VPL nucleus receives input from the spinothalamic tract and the posterior column-medial lemniscus pathway (body sensation: pain, temperature, touch, proprioception, vibration) and relays it to the somatosensory cortex.
The MGN relays auditory information from the inferior colliculus to the auditory cortex, not somatosensory information.
The LGN relays visual information from CN II to the visual cortex, not somatosensory information.
The VPM nucleus relays facial sensation and taste (via trigeminal and gustatory afferents), not body sensation.
questions.overview: The thalamus serves as the sensory (and motor) relay to the cortex; the VPL nucleus relays body somatosensory information via the spinothalamic and dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathways, while VPM relays facial sensation/taste, LGN relays vision, and MGN relays hearing — each projecting to its respective primary cortical area.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presents with sudden-onset vertigo, nausea, and vomiting. He also reports hoarseness and difficulty swallowing. On examination he has left-sided ptosis and miosis, loss of pain and temperature sensation over the left side of his face, loss of pain and temperature sensation over the right arm and leg, and a diminished gag reflex on the left. Which of the following is most likely occluded?
explanations: The anterior spinal artery supplies the medial medulla (corticospinal tract, medial lemniscus, CN XII), causing contralateral hemiparesis and tongue deviation, not this lateral medullary constellation.
AICA supplies the lateral pons and causes facial nerve palsy and hearing loss, not the dysphagia, hoarseness, and gag impairment seen here, which localize to the medulla.

This would produce the same syndrome but on the right side; this patient's Horner's syndrome, facial pain/temperature loss, and bulbar weakness are all left-sided, indicating a left-sided lesion, not right.
The MCA supplies the cortex and produces cortical signs such as aphasia or hemineglect, not brainstem findings like Horner's syndrome or crossed sensory loss.

Correct — a left PICA stroke causes left lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome: ipsilateral Horner's syndrome (descending sympathetic tract), ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss (spinal trigeminal nucleus), contralateral body pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic tract), ipsilateral hoarseness/dysphagia (nucleus ambiguus), and vertigo/nystagmus (vestibular nuclei).
questions.overview: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome results from PICA occlusion, damaging the vestibular nuclei, spinothalamic tract, spinal trigeminal nucleus, nucleus ambiguus, and descending sympathetic fibers, while sparing the medially located motor pathways. This produces ipsilateral face plus contralateral body sensory loss, ipsilateral Horner's syndrome, ipsilateral bulbar weakness (hoarseness, dysphagia), and vertigo/ataxia — remembered as 'Don't PICA a horse that can't eat.'

questions.stem: A patient recently started on both an SSRI and an MAOI develops agitation, diaphoresis, hyperthermia, tremor, and hyperreflexia. Which finding helps distinguish this condition from neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
explanations: Altered mental status occurs in both conditions and is not distinguishing.
Autonomic instability occurs in both conditions and is not a distinguishing feature.
Fever occurs in both serotonin syndrome and neuroleptic malignant syndrome and does not distinguish between them.

Correct — clonus and hyperreflexia are characteristic neuromuscular findings of serotonin syndrome (from excess serotonergic activity), whereas neuroleptic malignant syndrome (from dopamine blockade) classically presents with 'lead-pipe' rigidity rather than clonus.
questions.overview: Serotonin syndrome results from excess serotonergic activity (e.g., combining SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, or TCAs) and presents with the triad of mental status changes, autonomic hyperactivity, and neuromuscular abnormalities including clonus and hyperreflexia; it is distinguished from neuroleptic malignant syndrome (caused by dopamine blockade, with 'lead-pipe' rigidity and elevated CK) by the presence of clonus. Treatment of serotonin syndrome is cyproheptadine.

questions.stem: Activation of D1 receptors on striatal neurons stimulates the direct pathway of the basal ganglia. What is the net effect on movement?
explanations: Correct — D1 receptor activation stimulates the direct pathway, increasing striatal GABAergic inhibition of the GPi/SNr, which releases (disinhibits) the thalamus so it can activate the cortex, promoting movement.
The direct pathway ultimately disinhibits, not increases inhibition of, the cortex via the thalamus.
The direct pathway does affect movement — it promotes it via thalamic disinhibition.
Decreased movement via thalamic inhibition describes the (dopamine-suppressed) indirect pathway, not the D1-activated direct pathway.
questions.overview: Dopamine promotes movement by simultaneously activating the direct pathway (via D1 receptors, which disinhibits the thalamus and stimulates the motor cortex) and inhibiting the indirect pathway (via D2 receptors, which would otherwise inhibit the thalamus). Loss of dopaminergic neurons, as in Parkinson disease, tips the balance toward indirect pathway dominance, causing hypokinesia.

questions.stem: A patient has unilateral hearing loss. The Weber test lateralizes to the affected ear, and the Rinne test shows bone conduction greater than air conduction in that ear. What type of hearing loss is present?
explanations: Central auditory processing disorder is not assessed by the Weber/Rinne tests, which evaluate peripheral conductive versus sensorineural pathways.

Correct — in conductive hearing loss, Weber lateralizes to the bad (affected) ear because bone-conducted sound isn't masked by ambient noise there, and Rinne shows bone conduction greater than air conduction because sound cannot be conducted normally through the middle ear ossicles.
Mixed hearing loss would show intermediate findings, not the classic pattern of lateralization to the bad ear plus bone greater than air conduction seen in pure conductive loss.
In sensorineural hearing loss, Weber lateralizes to the good ear, and Rinne shows air conduction greater than bone conduction (though both reduced) — the opposite of this presentation.
questions.overview: The Weber test (tuning fork on the forehead) and Rinne test (comparing bone vs. air conduction) distinguish conductive from sensorineural hearing loss: conductive loss causes Weber to lateralize to the bad ear and bone conduction greater than air conduction (Rinne) in that ear, while sensorineural loss causes Weber to lateralize to the good ear with air conduction remaining greater than bone conduction.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of the 'worst headache of her life,' photophobia, and neck stiffness, without focal neurologic deficits. Initial CT head is negative. Lumbar puncture shows xanthochromia. Which of the following best describes the most likely source of bleeding and its known association?
options: Rupture of a berry aneurysm at the anterior communicating artery, associated with ADPKD
Middle meningeal artery rupture, associated with temporal bone fracture
Bridging vein rupture, associated with anticoagulation
AVM rupture, associated with neurofibromatosis type 1
Rupture of a Charcot-Bouchard aneurysm, associated with diabetes
explanations: Correct — the anterior communicating artery is the most common site of berry aneurysm rupture, causing subarachnoid hemorrhage (sudden 'worst headache,' meningismus, xanthochromia on LP). Berry aneurysms are associated with ADPKD, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and aortic coarctation.
Middle meningeal artery rupture causes epidural hematoma from trauma, typically with a lucid interval, not spontaneous SAH.
Bridging vein rupture causes subdural hematoma, a slow venous bleed with a crescent shape on CT, not SAH with xanthochromia.
AVMs are a rare cause of SAH but are not specifically associated with NF1 in these notes; a berry aneurysm with its ADPKD association fits this scenario best.
Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms are microscopic, associated with hypertension, and cause intraparenchymal (not subarachnoid) hemorrhage with focal deficits, not this presentation.
questions.overview: Subarachnoid hemorrhage is most often caused by rupture of a berry (saccular) aneurysm, classically at the anterior communicating artery, presenting with sudden 'thunderclap' headache, meningismus, and photophobia, with usually preserved neurologic function since blood flow to brain tissue is maintained. CT is most sensitive within 6 hours; if negative but suspicion remains high, LP showing xanthochromia confirms the diagnosis. Berry aneurysms are associated with ADPKD, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and aortic coarctation.

questions.stem: A patient can comprehend spoken language normally but produces short, halting, effortful speech and cannot express desired words. Which region is most likely damaged?
explanations: Correct — Broca's area, in the left frontal lobe, controls speech production; its destruction causes expressive (non-fluent) aphasia with intact comprehension but effortful, halting, 'broken' speech.
Wernicke's area damage (left temporal lobe) causes fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension — the opposite pattern from this patient's intact comprehension.
Right parietal lobe damage causes spatial neglect/agnosia, not a language production deficit.
Bilateral frontal injury (e.g., Phineas Gage) causes personality change and disinhibition, not isolated expressive aphasia.
questions.overview: Broca's area (left frontal lobe) governs speech production; its destruction causes non-fluent (expressive) aphasia with preserved comprehension but halting, effortful speech. Wernicke's area (left temporal lobe) governs speech comprehension; its destruction causes fluent but meaningless (receptive) aphasia. Damage to both produces global aphasia, often from a large MCA stroke.

questions.stem: A patient with vertigo has purely vertical nystagmus that changes direction with gaze, along with skew deviation of the eyes. Which of the following is most consistent with this presentation?
options: Central vertigo (e.g., brainstem or cerebellar lesion)
explanations: BPPV is a peripheral cause producing mixed horizontal/torsional nystagmus with delayed onset on positional testing (Dix-Hallpike), not purely vertical, direction-changing nystagmus.
Meniere's disease is peripheral, presenting with the triad of tinnitus, sensorineural hearing loss, and vertigo, not vertical or direction-changing nystagmus with skew deviation.
Vestibular neuritis is peripheral, causing horizontal nystagmus without the central red-flag features described.

Correct — purely vertical nystagmus, direction-changing nystagmus with gaze, and skew deviation are red flags for central vertigo (a brainstem or cerebellar lesion, e.g., stroke), distinguishing it from peripheral causes.
questions.overview: Distinguishing central from peripheral vertigo is critical: central vertigo (brainstem/cerebellar lesion) features purely vertical or direction-changing nystagmus, skew deviation, immediate-onset positional nystagmus, and other CNS signs (dysmetria, weakness), while peripheral vertigo (BPPV, vestibular neuritis, Meniere's) features horizontal/torsional nystagmus, delayed and fatigable positional nystagmus, and no other neurologic findings.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman experiences sudden painful monocular vision loss that worsens with eye movement, along with decreased color perception and an afferent pupillary defect. Weeks later she develops diplopia on left lateral gaze, with failure of her right eye to adduct and nystagmus of the abducting left eye. MRI shows periventricular white matter lesions. Which of the following best explains her presentation?
options: Multiple sclerosis; internuclear ophthalmoplegia from medial longitudinal fasciculus demyelination
explanations: Wernicke encephalopathy (thiamine deficiency) causes ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and confusion but not optic neuritis or periventricular plaques on MRI.
Central pontine myelinolysis follows rapid correction of hyponatremia and causes quadriparesis/locked-in features, not this optic neuritis plus INO presentation.
Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable ptosis/diplopia without an afferent pupillary defect or periventricular demyelinating lesions.
GBS is a peripheral nerve/nerve root demyelinating disease causing ascending weakness, not optic neuritis or internuclear ophthalmoplegia, and it does not produce periventricular MRI lesions.

Correct — this patient's optic neuritis (painful monocular vision loss, color desaturation, afferent pupillary defect) followed by internuclear ophthalmoplegia (failure of adduction of one eye with nystagmus of the contralateral abducting eye, from medial longitudinal fasciculus demyelination) with periventricular white matter lesions on MRI is classic for multiple sclerosis.
questions.overview: Multiple sclerosis is a CNS autoimmune demyelinating disease of young adults (female predominance) presenting with episodic neurologic deficits separated in time and space; classic presentations include optic neuritis (painful monocular vision loss with an afferent pupillary defect) and internuclear ophthalmoplegia (impaired adduction of one eye with nystagmus of the contralateral abducting eye from medial longitudinal fasciculus demyelination). MRI shows periventricular white matter plaques (Dawson's fingers), and CSF often shows oligoclonal bands.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is found unresponsive after a fall. Head CT shows a large right temporal epidural hematoma. On examination the right pupil is dilated and nonreactive, and there is left-sided hemiparesis. Which of the following best explains this exam finding?
options: Compression of the medulla through the foramen magnum
Compression of the right (ipsilateral) CN III as it herniates through the tentorial notch
Compression of the left (contralateral) CN III
Compression of the anterior cerebral artery under the falx cerebri
explanations: Pituitary stalk compression is not a described mechanism of the herniation syndromes tested here.
Compression of the medulla through the foramen magnum describes tonsillar herniation, which presents with respiratory/cardiac collapse, not a unilateral blown pupil.

Correct — the right temporal lobe (uncus) herniates medially through the tentorial notch, compressing the ipsilateral (right) CN III (causing an ipsilateral dilated, 'blown' pupil and ptosis) and the contralateral cerebral peduncle (causing contralateral, left, hemiparesis) — the classic findings of uncal herniation from an expanding epidural hematoma.
The dilated, nonreactive pupil is ipsilateral to the herniating temporal lobe (right), not the left CN III.
ACA compression under the falx cerebri occurs in subfalcine herniation, which causes contralateral leg weakness, not a blown pupil.
questions.overview: Uncal (transtentorial) herniation is a classic complication of an expanding mass like an epidural hematoma; the medial temporal lobe (uncus) pushes through the tentorial notch, compressing the ipsilateral CN III (an early sign is a 'blown,' dilated, nonreactive pupil with ptosis) and the cerebral peduncle, usually causing contralateral hemiparesis (though late compression against the tentorium can cause ipsilateral weakness — Kernohan's phenomenon).

questions.stem: Stroking the sole of the foot produces dorsiflexion of the great toe with fanning of the other toes in an adult. This finding indicates dysfunction of which pathway?
explanations: The dorsal columns carry vibration/proprioception; their damage would not produce an abnormal plantar reflex.
Peripheral nerve (LMN) lesions cause absent reflexes, not the pathologic extensor plantar response seen with corticospinal tract lesions.

Correct — a positive Babinski sign (dorsiflexion of the great toe with fanning) indicates loss of corticospinal tract inhibition, an upper motor neuron sign; it is normal in infants under 12 months due to incomplete myelination but abnormal thereafter.
The spinothalamic tract carries pain/temperature sensation and is not responsible for producing or suppressing the Babinski reflex.
questions.overview: The Babinski sign (dorsiflexion of the great toe with fanning of the other toes upon plantar stimulation) is a sign of upper motor neuron/corticospinal tract dysfunction in adults; it is physiologically present in infants under 12 months due to incomplete corticospinal myelination and becomes pathologic once it persists or reappears later in life.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man living in a college dormitory presents with fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and a petechial rash. Lumbar puncture reveals an elevated opening pressure, a cell count predominantly of neutrophils, elevated protein, and low glucose. Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci. Which of the following identifies the organism and the appropriate empiric therapy?
explanations: H. influenzae is a gram-negative rod (coccobacillus), not a diplococcus, and meningitis from it is now rare due to vaccination.

Correct — N. meningitidis is a gram-negative diplococcus that causes outbreaks in crowded settings like college dormitories and can cause meningococcemia with a petechial/purpuric rash; empiric therapy in young adults (6-60 years) is ceftriaxone plus vancomycin (to cover resistant S. pneumoniae) pending cultures.
Group B strep is a gram-positive coccus in chains and is the most common cause of neonatal meningitis, not appropriate for a 19-year-old with this presentation.
Listeria is a gram-positive rod typically seen in neonates, the elderly, or immunocompromised patients, not in a young healthy adult with a purpuric rash and gram-negative diplococci on stain.

S. pneumoniae is a gram-positive, lancet-shaped diplococcus in pairs, not the gram-negative diplococcus described, and vancomycin should be added empirically to cover possible cephalosporin resistance.
questions.overview: Neisseria meningitidis is a gram-negative diplococcus transmitted by respiratory droplets that causes outbreaks in crowded settings (dorms, barracks) and can progress to meningococcemia with a petechial/purpuric rash, DIC, and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (adrenal hemorrhage). Bacterial meningitis CSF shows elevated opening pressure, PMN pleocytosis, high protein, and low glucose; empiric treatment in adolescents/young adults is ceftriaxone plus vancomycin.

questions.stem: A patient with cocaine intoxication presents with chest pain, tachycardia, and hypertension. Why should beta-blockers be avoided in this setting?
options: Beta-blockers worsen cocaine's local anesthetic effect
Unopposed alpha-1 stimulation can worsen hypertension and coronary vasospasm
explanations: Cocaine's local anesthetic effect (sodium channel blockade) is a separate mechanism unrelated to beta-blocker administration.
Beta-blockers are not associated with precipitating serotonin syndrome; that risk is with serotonergic drugs like SSRIs/MAOIs.

Correct — cocaine blocks reuptake of norepinephrine, causing massive alpha and beta stimulation; blocking beta receptors leaves alpha-1 vasoconstriction unopposed, worsening hypertension and coronary vasospasm (chest pain).
Beta-blockers do not affect dopamine reuptake; cocaine itself blocks reuptake of dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin.
questions.overview: Cocaine blocks presynaptic reuptake of norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin, causing generalized sympathetic activation with tachycardia, hypertension, and coronary vasospasm; beta-blockers are avoided because blocking beta-2-mediated vasodilation leaves alpha-1 vasoconstriction unopposed, worsening hypertension and cardiac ischemia. First-line treatment for cocaine toxicity is benzodiazepines.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with three months of progressive diplopia and ptosis that worsen throughout the day and improve with rest. She also reports difficulty chewing tough foods. Deep tendon reflexes are normal. Chest CT shows an anterior mediastinal mass. Which of the following is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
explanations: Creatine kinase is normal in both myasthenia gravis and LEMS; an elevated CK would instead suggest a myopathy.
Anti-VGCC antibodies are diagnostic of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, which improves (not worsens) with muscle use and is linked to small cell lung cancer rather than a thymic mass.

Correct — myasthenia gravis is caused by autoantibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. AChR antibody testing is the key diagnostic test, and MG is strongly associated with thymic hyperplasia or thymoma, explaining this patient's anterior mediastinal mass.
Segmental demyelination on nerve biopsy suggests a peripheral demyelinating neuropathy (such as GBS), not a postsynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder like myasthenia gravis.
Albuminocytologic dissociation (elevated CSF protein with a normal cell count) is characteristic of Guillain-Barre syndrome, not myasthenia gravis.
questions.overview: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder caused by antibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, producing fatigable weakness that worsens with repeated muscle use (a decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation) and classically presenting with ptosis/diplopia and bulbar symptoms. It is strongly associated with thymic hyperplasia or thymoma, and thymectomy often improves symptoms.

questions.stem: A patient has increased muscle tone, hyperreflexia, a positive Babinski sign, and no muscle atrophy or fasciculations. This pattern is most consistent with damage to which structure?
explanations: Correct — upper motor neuron lesions (corticospinal tract, e.g., cortex, internal capsule) cause spastic paralysis: increased tone, hyperreflexia, a positive Babinski sign, and no atrophy/fasciculations, since the lower motor neuron and muscle remain intact.
Peripheral nerve damage is also a lower motor neuron pattern, causing flaccid weakness and atrophy, not spasticity or a Babinski sign.
NMJ disorders (e.g., myasthenia gravis) cause fatigable weakness without changes in tone, reflexes, or a Babinski sign.
Anterior horn cell (LMN) damage causes flaccid weakness, hyporeflexia, muscle atrophy, and fasciculations — the opposite of the pattern described.
questions.overview: Upper motor neuron lesions (cortex, internal capsule, corticospinal tract) cause spastic paralysis: increased tone, hyperreflexia, a positive Babinski sign, and no atrophy or fasciculations. Lower motor neuron lesions (anterior horn cell, nerve root, peripheral nerve) cause flaccid paralysis: decreased tone, hyporeflexia/areflexia, muscle atrophy, and fasciculations — a key distinction for localizing neurologic lesions.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with two days of progressive symmetric ascending weakness that began in his legs and has now reached his forearms, three weeks after an episode of bloody diarrhea. He has diffuse areflexia and mild distal paresthesias. Vital signs show a heart rate of 118/min and blood pressure of 160/95 mmHg. Which of the following is the most important next step in management?
explanations: Nerve biopsy is not required for diagnosis and would delay the urgent respiratory assessment this patient needs.

Correct — Guillain-Barre syndrome can rapidly progress to respiratory failure from diaphragmatic weakness. Serial vital capacity or negative inspiratory force monitoring is critical to detect impending respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support; autonomic instability (tachycardia, hypertension) also requires close monitoring.
GBS is a clinical diagnosis supported by CSF albuminocytologic dissociation; lumbar spine MRI is not the priority in an acutely progressing patient at risk for respiratory failure.
Unlike many other inflammatory neuropathies, corticosteroids are not effective in GBS; treatment is plasmapheresis or IVIG.
Treating the preceding Campylobacter infection does not alter the course of GBS, which is already immune-mediated by the time neurologic symptoms appear.
questions.overview: Guillain-Barre syndrome is an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy, often triggered by molecular mimicry after infections like Campylobacter jejuni, causing ascending flaccid paralysis, areflexia, and autonomic instability with CSF albuminocytologic dissociation (elevated protein, normal cell count). Respiratory failure from diaphragmatic weakness is the most feared complication, so vital capacity should be monitored serially, and treatment is plasmapheresis or IVIG (not steroids).

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl has multiple daily brief episodes of staring and eyelid fluttering lasting a few seconds with no postictal confusion. EEG shows generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges. Which drug is first-line treatment?
explanations: Valproate can treat absence seizures but is not the first-line drug of choice; ethosuximide is preferred for isolated absence seizures given its more favorable side-effect profile.
Phenytoin (sodium channel blockade) is used for partial and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, not as the first-line choice for absence seizures.

Correct — ethosuximide, which blocks thalamic T-type calcium channels, is the first-line treatment for childhood absence seizures, which classically present with brief staring spells without postictal confusion and a 3-Hz spike-and-wave EEG pattern.
Carbamazepine is used for partial/generalized tonic-clonic seizures and trigeminal neuralgia; it is not first-line for absence seizures and can worsen some generalized seizure types.
questions.overview: Childhood absence epilepsy presents with brief (5-15 second) staring spells, eyelid fluttering, and no postictal confusion, with a classic 3-Hz spike-and-wave EEG pattern; it results from abnormal thalamic T-type calcium channel activity, and ethosuximide (a T-type calcium channel blocker) is the first-line treatment.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with longstanding, poorly controlled hypertension develops sudden dense right-sided weakness and sensory loss involving the face, arm, and leg equally, with gaze deviation to the left. Non-contrast CT shows a hyperdense lesion in the left basal ganglia. Which of the following is the most likely underlying vascular pathology?
options: Rupture of a Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysm from chronic hypertension
Rupture of a berry aneurysm at the anterior communicating artery
explanations: Embolism from atrial fibrillation causes ischemic (not hemorrhagic) stroke, typically in cortical MCA territory with cortical signs, not a hyperdense basal ganglia bleed.

Correct — chronic hypertension causes lipohyalinosis and Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms in small penetrating vessels (lenticulostriate branches of the MCA) supplying the basal ganglia/internal capsule; rupture causes hypertensive intraparenchymal hemorrhage with dense, equal face/arm/leg deficits, unlike cortical strokes.
Bridging vein rupture causes subdural hematoma, an extra-axial crescent-shaped bleed, not an intraparenchymal basal ganglia hemorrhage.
Cerebral amyloid angiopathy classically causes recurrent lobar hemorrhages in elderly patients, not basal ganglia hemorrhages.
Berry aneurysms at the AComm cause subarachnoid hemorrhage presenting with sudden severe headache and meningismus, not a basal ganglia parenchymal bleed with hemiparesis.
questions.overview: Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms arise from chronic hypertension-induced lipohyalinosis of small penetrating arteries (classically lenticulostriate branches of the MCA) and are the most common cause of hypertensive intraparenchymal hemorrhage, most often in the basal ganglia/internal capsule. Because the internal capsule carries all descending motor fibers together, these bleeds cause 'dense,' equal face/arm/leg weakness, unlike cortical strokes.

questions.stem: Which structure lies outside the blood-brain barrier and functions as the chemoreceptor trigger zone for vomiting?
options: OVLT (organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis)
explanations: The OVLT contains osmosensory neurons that detect blood osmolality, unrelated to the vomiting reflex.
The median eminence of the hypothalamus releases hormones to regulate the pituitary gland, not a vomiting center.
The subfornical organ responds to circulating substances like angiotensin II but is not the chemoreceptor trigger zone for emesis.

Correct — the area postrema, at the caudal end of the 4th ventricle, is a circumventricular organ outside the BBB that serves as the chemoreceptor trigger zone, detecting circulating toxins/chemotherapy agents and signaling the medullary vomiting center.
questions.overview: Circumventricular organs (area postrema, OVLT, subfornical organ, median eminence) lack a blood-brain barrier, allowing them to sense or secrete substances directly into or from the bloodstream. The area postrema specifically acts as the chemoreceptor trigger zone, detecting circulating toxins (including chemotherapy agents) and triggering vomiting via the medullary vomiting center.

questions.stem: Fibers of the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway carrying vibration and proprioception decussate at which level?
explanations: The pathway does decussate — just at a higher level (the medulla) than the spinothalamic tract.
Decussation of this pathway occurs in the medulla, not the midbrain.
Unlike the spinothalamic tract, which decussates at the spinal cord level of entry, the posterior columns do not cross until the medulla.

Correct — posterior column fibers ascend ipsilaterally in the spinal cord and synapse in the nucleus gracilis/cuneatus of the medulla, where second-order neurons decussate before ascending as the medial lemniscus to the thalamus.
questions.overview: The dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway (vibration, proprioception, fine touch) ascends ipsilaterally in the spinal cord and decussates in the medulla at the nucleus gracilis/cuneatus, whereas the spinothalamic tract (pain, temperature, crude touch) decussates immediately at the spinal cord level of entry — both tracts cross, but at different levels, which is key for localizing spinal cord versus brainstem lesions.

questions.stem: Epinephrine is the drug of choice for anaphylaxis primarily because of which combination of receptor effects?
options: Beta-2 mediated bronchodilation and alpha-1 mediated vasoconstriction
Beta-1 mediated increased heart rate only
explanations: Correct — epinephrine treats anaphylaxis via beta-2 agonism causing bronchodilation (reversing wheezing) and alpha-1 agonism causing vasoconstriction (reversing hypotension/vasodilation), addressing both bronchospasm and shock simultaneously.
Beta-1 effects raise heart rate and cardiac output but do not address the bronchoconstriction and vasodilation that make anaphylaxis life-threatening.
Alpha-2 agonism is a CNS effect that reduces sympathetic outflow and would worsen, not treat, anaphylactic shock.
Beta-2 mediated vasodilation would worsen hypotension; epinephrine's alpha-1 effect counteracts this in the vasculature while beta-2 dilates airways.
questions.overview: Epinephrine is the treatment of choice for anaphylaxis because at treatment doses it acts on both beta-2 receptors (bronchodilation, reversing wheezing) and alpha-1 receptors (vasoconstriction, reversing hypotension and vasodilation), simultaneously treating the two life-threatening features of anaphylactic shock.

questions.stem: Which glial cell type myelinates multiple CNS axons and is destroyed in multiple sclerosis?
explanations: Correct — oligodendrocytes myelinate multiple central axons (unlike Schwann cells, which myelinate only one peripheral axon each) and are the target of autoimmune destruction in multiple sclerosis.
Microglia are CNS macrophages that respond to injury and infection (e.g., HIV encephalitis) but do not produce myelin.
Astrocytes support neurons, form the glial scar after injury, and produce GFAP, but they do not myelinate axons.
Schwann cells myelinate peripheral axons (one cell per axon) and are destroyed in Guillain-Barre syndrome, not multiple sclerosis.
questions.overview: Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons (each myelinating multiple axons) and are destroyed in multiple sclerosis, while Schwann cells myelinate PNS axons (one axon per cell) and are destroyed in Guillain-Barre syndrome; myelin increases conduction velocity via saltatory conduction, allowing depolarization to jump between the Nodes of Ranvier.

questions.stem: Which G-protein subtype is coupled to alpha-1 and M3 receptors, mediating smooth muscle contraction via increased IP3 and intracellular calcium?
explanations: Gi-coupled receptors (M2, alpha-2) inhibit adenylyl cyclase, decreasing cAMP, and are associated with cardiac inhibition, not IP3-mediated smooth muscle contraction.
Gt (transducin) mediates visual phototransduction, not autonomic smooth muscle signaling.

Correct — Gq-coupled receptors (alpha-1, M1, M3) activate phospholipase C, increasing IP3 and intracellular calcium, causing smooth muscle contraction such as vasoconstriction, bronchoconstriction, and detrusor contraction.
Gs-coupled receptors (beta-1, beta-2) stimulate adenylyl cyclase, raising cAMP, causing cardiac stimulation or smooth muscle relaxation, not contraction via IP3.
questions.overview: G-protein coupled adrenergic and muscarinic receptors fall into three main classes: Gq (alpha-1, M1, M3) activates phospholipase C to raise IP3/calcium and contract smooth muscle; Gs (beta-1, beta-2, D1) stimulates adenylyl cyclase to raise cAMP; and Gi (alpha-2, M2, D2) inhibits adenylyl cyclase to lower cAMP, generally producing inhibitory effects like decreased heart rate.

questions.stem: Following a moderate peripheral nerve crush injury (axonotmesis), the axon and myelin sheath distal to the injury site degenerate. What is this process called?
explanations: Neurotmesis is a severity classification (complete disruption of axon, myelin, and connective tissue continuity), not the term for the distal degeneration process itself.
Chromatolysis refers to changes in the cell body (soma swelling, peripheral nucleus displacement, dispersed Nissl substance) proximal to the injury, not the distal degeneration process.
Neurapraxia is the mildest nerve injury (focal demyelination with an intact axon), which does not involve Wallerian degeneration.

Correct — Wallerian degeneration is the process by which the axon and myelin sheath degenerate distal to (and slightly proximal to) a site of axonal injury; regrowth may occur if the Schwann cell basal lamina remains intact.
questions.overview: After axonal injury (axonotmesis or worse), the axon and myelin distal to the lesion undergo Wallerian degeneration, while the cell body undergoes chromatolysis (edema, peripheral nucleus, dispersed Nissl substance) as it ramps up protein synthesis for repair; regrowth is possible if Schwann cells maintain their basal lamina scaffold.

questions.stem: A patient has contralateral hemiparesis of the face, arm, and leg, contralateral loss of vibration/proprioception, and ipsilateral tongue deviation with flaccid paralysis. Which artery is most likely occluded?
explanations: Posterior communicating artery aneurysms classically cause an isolated CN III palsy, unrelated to medullary motor/tongue syndromes.
PICA occlusion causes lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, with ipsilateral face pain/temperature loss, Horner's syndrome, and dysphagia/hoarseness — not this motor and tongue pattern.
AICA supplies the lateral pons, causing facial weakness and hearing loss, not the medullary tongue findings described.

Correct — this is medial medullary syndrome, caused by anterior spinal artery occlusion, damaging the corticospinal tract (contralateral hemiparesis), medial lemniscus (contralateral vibration/proprioception loss), and CN XII (ipsilateral flaccid tongue paralysis, deviating toward the lesion).
questions.overview: By the 'Rule of 4s,' midline (medial) brainstem structures include the motor pathway (corticospinal tract, causing contralateral weakness), medial lemniscus (contralateral vibration/proprioception loss), and cranial nerve nuclei divisible by 12 (III, IV, VI, XII), which cause ipsilateral cranial nerve weakness. Medial medullary syndrome (CN XII plus corticospinal/lemniscal involvement) results from anterior spinal artery occlusion.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman develops sudden right-sided weakness of the face, arm, and leg. On examination her left eye is ptotic, deviated down and out, with a dilated, nonreactive pupil. Which of the following best explains her presentation?
options: Left posterior cerebral artery infarct of the ventral midbrain
Left basilar artery infarct of the pons
Left vertebral artery infarct of the medulla
Right posterior cerebral artery infarct of the ventral midbrain
explanations: Correct — Weber syndrome is a ventral midbrain infarct in the PCA territory that damages the exiting CN III fibers (ipsilateral, here left, oculomotor palsy: ptosis, eye down and out, dilated pupil) and the corticospinal tract in the cerebral peduncle (contralateral, here right, hemiparesis).
A pontine basilar artery stroke would produce CN VI or VII findings, not the CN III palsy described here, since CN III originates in the midbrain, not the pons.
A vertebral artery stroke of the medulla (anterior spinal territory) causes CN XII findings (tongue deviation), not a CN III palsy.

A right-sided lesion would cause a right CN III palsy and left hemiparesis; this patient has a left CN III palsy (left eye down and out, dilated pupil) with right hemiparesis, indicating a left-sided lesion.
An MCA stroke produces cortical signs (aphasia, neglect) and face/arm-predominant weakness, not an oculomotor nerve palsy.
questions.overview: Weber syndrome is a ventral midbrain stroke (PCA branches) that damages the exiting oculomotor nerve fibers (ipsilateral CN III palsy: eye down-and-out, ptosis, dilated pupil) and the corticospinal tract in the cerebral peduncle (contralateral hemiparesis). It contrasts with Benedikt syndrome, which involves the more dorsal red nucleus and causes contralateral tremor/ataxia instead of hemiparesis.
